title: AI-drafted time entries from captured activity, reviewed by the professional
problem: Time is often written from memory at day or week end, so short tasks are missed and recording time is itself unbillable work.
approach: A capture layer records email, document, call and application activity and drafts entries by matter; the professional reviews and releases each one.
Laurel customers include Lerners, Tonkon Torp, Berger Singerman and GHJ; Lerners reports +0.48 billable hours per lawyer daily (vendor-published).
An unnamed Big Four tax division reported +2.3 chargeable hours per timekeeper weekly against a control group (vendor-published).
Billing partner review of the resulting bill remains an existing step.
who: Lerners, Tonkon Torp, Berger Singerman, GHJ, Laurel

title: Work done in AI platforms becomes draft time entries for lawyer review
problem: As more work moves into AI platforms, it is hard to capture and easy to leave off the timesheet, and leaders want to see what AI work returns.
approach: The AI platform passes completed tasks to timekeeping, which drafts an entry with matter, duration and narrative; the lawyer reviews and submits.
Aderant announced an iTimekeep integration with Harvey as live on 2026-08-17; Laurel and Legora announced Legora tasks becoming draft entries on 2026-10-13.
Litify and Thomson Reuters announced similar capture. These are announcements; no results published (vendor-published).
who: Aderant, Laurel, Legora, Litify, Thomson Reuters

title: Client billing guidelines turned into rules checked as entries are written
problem: Client billing guidelines run 15 to 100 pages each, are impossible to remember across hundreds of clients, and clients reject non-compliant invoices.
approach: Guidelines become rules an administrator approves; each entry is checked as written, with suggested narratives and codes the timekeeper accepts or edits.
Intapp released work-code prediction in May 2026; Laurel, Elite and Aderant (early access) announced similar features.
One unnamed Laurel customer cut pre-bill review time 30-40% (vendor-published); Intapp claims 75% faster time entry release (vendor-published).

title: Linklaters' firm-built tool checks time-entry narratives in bulk before billing
problem: Reviewing narrative time entries for the wrong workstream, typos and non-compliance with client requirements is laborious.
approach: Linklaters' Narrative Checker, an Excel plugin, sends narratives to the firm's in-house chatbot to find common issues and propose corrections.
A managing associate built it as a side project; it was piloted globally and released firm-wide on 1 September.
Builder says about a thousand narratives a minute, over 300 uses in a week (self-reported). Users accept or reject each correction.

title: AI checks pre-bills against client guidelines; a partner accepts or rejects fixes
problem: Partners spend huge amounts of time reviewing pre-bills each month, and invoice rejection rates are rising.
approach: Foley Mansfield went live firmwide with Verify from Zero Systems, which flags pre-bill entries breaking guideline rules and suggests one-click fixes.
Foley's managing partner says reviewing highlighted items replaced days of review with minutes (self-reported).
Zero Systems' CEO claims about 6% of revenue otherwise written off is recovered (vendor-published).
Billing partner or biller accepts or dismisses each flag and signs off the bill.

title: AI ranks draft-bill edits so reviewers focus on high-impact bills
problem: Lawyers and billing teams review and adjust draft bills before invoices go out, and Elite describes routine review decisions as repetitive.
approach: Elite added Elite Intelligence to the Proforma workflow in 3E, reported 2026-02-27; it prioritises edits and highlights high-impact proformas.
Elite expects up to 4 hours saved per month per lawyer; an expectation, not a measurement (vendor-published).
Lawyers and billing teams still review and adjust draft bills.

title: Scope-creep flags on fixed-fee matters while the bill is assembled
problem: On fixed-fee matters, work outside the engagement is absorbed as a write-down at close instead of raised as a change order.
approach: Laurel Billing's Scope agent will track budget burn against the engagement and flag drifted hours in dollars, each with a proposed fix.
Approved corrections feed back into timekeeping.
Billing or matter partner approves or dismisses each flag and decides whether to raise a change order. No results published (vendor-published).

title: Idea: score pre-bills for write-down risk before the bill goes out
problem: Idea, not a deployment: write-downs happen late and unevenly; 43% of partners always or usually reduce bills when time exceeds their expectations.
approach: Idea. Use historical realization, client guidelines and AI bill analysis to flag entries and matters likely to be reduced before invoicing.
Perlin argues GenAI could help firms predict task and matter costs; no deployment was found.
Billing partner decides adjustments, as today. No figures published.

title: AI drafts appeals for rejected e-billing invoices and ranks which to pursue
problem: Billers manage dozens of client e-billing platforms and appeals departments chase payments on appeals that leaders call mostly unfair and unsuccessful.
approach: Aderant's Appeals Agent identifies and prioritises high-value appeal opportunities after e-billing rejections and drafts supporting rationale (announced 2026-05-12; early access 2026-08-25).
Billing team reviews each drafted appeal before submission.
No results published (vendor-published).

title: AI prioritises overdue accounts by payment risk and drafts follow-ups for staff
problem: Collections teams spend hours each week drafting follow-ups and deciding whom to chase and in what tone.
approach: Aderant's Collections Agent prioritises accounts and recommends outreach (early access 2026-08-25); Oddr released AI-drafted collection emails with tone controls.
Oddr says a Collections Agent in development will draft emails or call briefs; Certinia positions its Veda agents for services firms.
Certinia's page claims 24 days faster from delivery to payment, basis not stated (vendor-published). Collections staff decide what is sent.

title: Overdue invoices chased automatically, with human collectors for calls and escalations
problem: Law firms take on average 97 days to get paid, per Clio data cited by CollBox, and no one owns accounts receivable.
approach: CollBox integrates with practice management systems, detects unpaid bills and chases them with email reminders and calls from trained accounts-receivable specialists.
CollBox claims more than $100 million recovered for law firms in the past year (vendor-published; basis not stated).
Trained collectors make calls and handle escalations.

title: Time capture extended to executives and administrative staff for cost to serve
problem: At GHJ, firm-services teams and executives had no time system, so leadership could not see resource allocation or whether workloads were sustainable.
approach: After piloting Laurel and expanding it firmwide, GHJ is rolling it out to firm-services and administrative staff who never tracked time.
It intends to use the data for resource allocation and hiring evidence.
GHJ's Chief of Staff says it shows how her time is spent; no firm-level results (self-reported). Staff review their own entries.

title: In-house teams use AI to review every outside-counsel invoice against guidelines
problem: Albertsons works with about 180 outside law firms, and invoices with hundreds of line items make problems easy to miss.
approach: Albertsons uses Thomson Reuters Legal Tracker's AI audit to flag invoice lines, plus automated volume discounts; Brightflag and Onit offer similar tools.
Albertsons' program manager says the audit and discount together saved 'probably almost $2 million' year to date (self-reported).
Onit claims 92% invoice-level accuracy against 72% for experienced lawyers (vendor-published). An in-house reviewer approves, rejects or amends flagged invoices.

title: Idea: tag AI-assisted work in time entries and check against client terms
problem: Idea, not a deployment: client terms already ask for AI use to be noted in time entries, and some clients will not pay for AI work.
approach: Idea. The timekeeping tool or AI platform records AI-assisted tasks; billing checks them against client AI terms and fee rules before invoicing.
Zscaler's guidelines already require noting generative AI use in the time entry. No firm or vendor describes this check.
Timekeeper confirms the AI tag; billing partner applies the client rule and judges flat-fee reasonableness.

title: Idea: a summarised 'services rendered' invoice in place of itemised time
problem: Idea, not a deployment: when AI compresses hours into minutes, an itemised hourly bill may undersell the value delivered.
approach: Idea. At Legalweek 2026, Zarwin Baum's Mitchell Kaplan suggested a single 'services rendered' line and asked whether clients would accept it.
No AI tool writes such a summary and no firm has adopted the format.
Billing partner agrees the format with the client.

title: Consulting firms use platform agents to complete, chase and check timesheets
problem: Certinia describes timekeeping as a chronically low-adoption workflow, leading to less compliance and more unbilled time.
approach: Certinia's Veda positions conversational timekeeping; its Project Assistant Agent, in early adoption, flags missing time cards to managers but creates no entries.
Kantata's Agent Studio lets practice leads describe agents in plain language; Basware is named as a user, with a statement of intent.
Project manager acts on flags; each person confirms their own time. No figures published (vendor-published).

title: Accounting firms use AI on time, unbilled work and invoices
problem: Time capture, unbilled work review, billing and collections at many accounting firms still run on spreadsheets and email, and few partners can pull realization on demand.
approach: Aiwyn's general manager says AI already changes time and billing through automated time capture, early flags of unbilled-work problems and predictive billing.
One unnamed firm cut finished-work-to-bill time from 29 to 18 days in a month; the article credits visibility, not AI (vendor-published).
A person reviews unbilled work before the bill goes out; no AI checkpoint is described.
